claim_to_evidence.computations: Exact integer sieve n<=1,000,000: 208 dyadic-totient candidates; 3 solutions.
critical_steps: Odd prime factors occur exactly once and are Fermat primes
Odd n gives T=2^(1-T)P, forcing a contradiction
Even n gives a-1+T=2^(2-T)P and hence T<=2
T=0,1,2 yield exactly 32,192,80 and are checked
claim_to_evidence.domain: All positive integers n with phi(n)=2^e, e>=0.
claim_to_evidence.unproved_limits: Nothing asserted when phi(n) has an odd prime factor; indexed search does not guarantee novelty; external independent audit not performed.

correctness.rationale: The exact proof handles n=1,2 separately, proves n=2^a times distinct Fermat primes when phi(n) is dyadic, and excludes odd n. For even n, writing T=sum 2^j and odd P=product(2^(2^j)+1), it proves a-1+T=2^(2-T)P; integrality implies T<=2. Its only three cases give n=32,192,80, each verified directly. No appeal to the finite test proves the universal quantifier. A standalone exact integer sieve checked every dyadic-totient n up to 1,000,000 and observed exactly these hits.

A248815 lists known witnesses but no such necessity theorem.

value.rationale: The natural dyadic-totient domain is precisely the Gauss-Wantzel constructible regular polygon index set for n>=3. The original derivative fixed-point sequence already includes examples 32,80,192. The theorem turns them into a complete all-size answer and excludes every potential contribution from as-yet-unknown higher Fermat primes, a structural unbounded classification rather than a table extension or arbitrary slice.
